title: Research design worksheet
text:
Answer in plain language. If you cannot answer one of these in a sentence or two, that is what to work on next. You will use this twice: for your own project, and to explain a classmate’s back to them in workshop 4.

What is your unit of observation? (Individuals? Leaders? Countries? Provinces, cities, districts? Country-years? Protests? Speeches?)


What is your dependent variable? Fifteen words or fewer.


What is your independent variable — the thing that causes a change in your dependent variable? This is your “treatment”, the cause of a change in the world. Fifteen words or fewer.


What variation do you expect to see in the dependent variable when the independent variable takes different values? What is the difference between “treated” units and “control” units? Two to four sentences.


Is there a mechanism — an intermediate step — between the independent variable changing and the dependent variable changing? Almost certainly yes. What is it? Put another way: what else has to happen for the effect of X to reach all the way to Y?


How will you measure the independent variable, in conceptual terms? How will you know whether a unit has been treated? What information about each unit do you need?


What is a treated unit like? What characteristic distinguishes it from an untreated one?


How will you measure the dependent variable, in conceptual terms? How will you collect information showing different outcomes for multiple units?


What else could produce the same pattern? Name one or two alternative explanations and what you would do about them (control for them, choose cases that hold them constant, show they do not fit).


Does X come before Y in time, in your data or cases? If the independent variable is measured after the outcome moved, something is wrong.

title: Capstone 2026-27: Authoritarianism theme
text:
1. The theme
You can study one authoritarian state in the present or recent past, compare two non-democracies, or use quantitative methods to compare across authoritarian systems. Topics include non-democratic institutions, the strategies of lesser-studied regimes, ideology, surveillance and information control, transitions (e.g. Myanmar, Venezuela), and the role of external actors.
Quantitative data on authoritarian elites, public opinion, economic performance and institutions is available, and I will strongly encourage using it — no one needs to be an R expert already, and I will help. Careful qualitative work is equally welcome. What matters is that the project is new, interesting, feasible, narrow, and political science rather than a report; we discuss these criteria in the first workshop.

title: Capstone 2026-27: Authoritarianism theme
text:
2. How the group works
Fortnightly two-hour workshops develop your independent research project: you present, get feedback from me and each other, act as discussant for someone else, and leave with a clearer next step. Between workshops you do the work.

Come prepared and contribute. Read what is assigned — academic readings early on, each other’s drafts later. Participation is assessed; I record attendance and contribution at every workshop.
This is your project. I can offer leads, advice, and course corrections.
One-to-one supervision is not part of this module. All supervision happens in workshops and clinics.


Clinics
Clinics are drop-in “group office hours” for concrete problems: your data, your R code, a paragraph that will not come right, a dataset you cannot find. These will be held in HT, dates TBA.

4. Assessment
The weights and the rules are set by the Overall Capstone Document; this section says what each piece looks like in our group.

Participation (10%)
Attend every workshop, engage with the material, present your own work at each stage, and act as a formal discussant for a classmate in Hilary Term. Unexcused absences reduce this mark. You must attend at least two workshops in each term to be permitted to submit a dissertation.


Short submissions (15%)
Four short pieces, each feeding the next, presented briefly in the following workshop. Word limits carry a 10% tolerance either way; outside that range costs up to 5 marks. Make each one as useful to you as you can.

Full specs, and what a good one looks like, are in the short-submissions sheet.


Research proposal (formative; compulsory)
1,500 words, due Friday 11 December, 5pm. Not marked, but you must submit it to be allowed to submit the dissertation, and you will get detailed written feedback. Include an introduction (topic, social and scholarly significance), a literature review, the variation to be explained, the main posited explanation(s), and the methodological strategy. You will work from this over the Christmas break — and you will need to.


Dissertation (65%)
The final research project: 8,000 words maximum, due Wednesday 24 March 2027 at 4pm via Turnitin. This limit is the department’s, not mine, and there is no tolerance on it — 10 marks deducted if exceeded — and a successful project is unlikely to be shorter than 7,500. Word count includes text and footnotes; excludes title page, abstract, acknowledgments, table of contents, tables, appendices and bibliography. House style: title page, abstract, table of contents, alphabetical bibliography, precise word count, and the School Assignment Submission Form as first page. Late work: 5 marks per day or part thereof; nothing accepted after Monday of Hilary teaching week 12.


Podcast (10%)
A 5–8 minute audio podcast explaining your project to a general audience — the question, why it matters, what others have found, your explanation, your findings and what they mean — due Friday 9 April 2027, 5pm. Assessed on substance and structure, not production values; any recording software is fine. If you can explain your dependent variable to a parent or friend with no political science, you are most of the way there.

title: Capstone 2026-27: Authoritarianism theme
text:
6. Readings
For workshop 1, look at these and come with reactions: what you liked, what you did not, ideas they sparked. You do not have to read every word.
Recommended

Milan Svolik. 2012. The Politics of Authoritarian Rule. Cambridge University Press. Chapter 1.
Andreas Schedler. 2002. “The Menu of Manipulation.” Journal of Democracy 13(2): 36–50.

Also recommended

Beatriz Magaloni. 2006. Voting for Autocracy. Cambridge University Press. Introduction and two chapters of your choice from 2–8.
Sheena Chestnut Greitens. 2016. Dictators and their Secret Police. Cambridge University Press. Selected pages.
Quintin H. Beazer, Noah Buckley and Ora John Reuter. 2026. “The Demand for Elections under Autocracy: Regime Approval and the Elimination of Local Elections in Russia.” American Journal of Political Science.

Research design (all year; the first two are on Blackboard)

Alan Bryman. 2016. Social Research Methods. Oxford University Press.
John Gerring. 2012. Social Science Methodology: A Unified Framework. Cambridge University Press.
Paul M. Kellstedt and Guy D. Whitten. 2018. The Fundamentals of Political Science Research. 3rd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Charles Lipson. 2005. How to Write a BA Thesis. University of Chicago Press.
Gary King, Robert O. Keohane and Sidney Verba. 1994. Designing Social Inquiry. Princeton University Press.

And the research guide: the pitfalls I see every year, collected in one place.

title: Capstone 2026-27: Authoritarianism theme
text:
7. Ethics approval
Research involving human participants (interviews, surveys, participant observation, experiments) needs approval from the Department of Political Science before data collection, and the review takes weeks. Retrospective approval is not possible. If you might collect original data from people, tell me at workshop 2 or 3 at the latest and apply by December (January in exceptional circumstances). Approval is not guaranteed, so have a back-up plan. Secondary analysis of existing data does not need clearance. Most projects in this group will not need it.

title: Capstone 2026-27: Authoritarianism theme
text:
8. Academic integrity
Plagiarism is a serious offence, and undisclosed AI-generated text counts. See the Library guide: libguides.tcd.ie/academic-integrity.

Generative AI
These tools exist, you use them, and you will use them in whatever you do after this degree. What this module assesses is whether you can ask a question, design a way to answer it, and write up what you found. So the line is: use these tools to help you think, to help you code, and to help you fix prose you wrote; do not use them to do the thinking or produce the prose. What is permitted for each piece of work is in the table below, in the vocabulary of the School Assignment Submission Form. “Permitted” means you may do it and must tick the corresponding box on the form. “Not permitted” means doing it is an academic integrity matter, whether or not you disclose it.

title: Presenting your work, and being a discussant
text:
Short and informal: about five minutes of you, then feedback, twelve minutes in total.

Maximum three substantive slides (one per idea, question or method). PowerPoint or PDF, uploaded to the group OneDrive folder by 8:40 on the morning of the workshop.
Slides are a barebones guide — to keep yourself on track and orient us, not to write down everything you think. Say your thoughts out loud; don’t paste in your document.
Few words per slide — you can’t read and listen at the same time. Give thought to what we need to know and what you can leave off.
Try to get across, for each idea: the outcome of interest and a potential explanation, the motivation, and the social and scholarly relevance. You may not have room for all of it; choose.
From workshop 3 on, add one slide of specific questions for the group. Be concrete: “Is V-Dem’s civil-liberties index too slow-moving to pick up the change I care about?” beats “any thoughts?”

title: Presenting your work, and being a discussant
text:
Presenting in Hilary (workshops 7 and 8)
A 10–12 minute presentation with slides, followed by your discussant (about five minutes), then open discussion.

Cover the basics — what you are doing and why — but be as specific as possible. Show a bit of the data, your survey, a graph of how things look, a first regression table, a case comparison table. Use the slides to your advantage.
Talk about what is not working: open questions, contingencies if the data do not cooperate, your best guess at exactly how you will analyse things.
Circulate a written draft by the Tuesday evening before you present, at the very latest. The more you send, the better the feedback: an improved and expanded proposal at minimum; a detailed outline is better; an early draft of the introduction and any other sections is best. It does not need to be polished or complete.

title: Presenting your work, and being a discussant
text:
Being a discussant
Every student is the assigned discussant for one classmate in Hilary.

Read the draft carefully, ahead of time, and write your comments down and organise them. Plan to speak for about five minutes.
Lead with what the project is trying to do, in your own words. If you cannot say it in two sentences, that is your first comment.
Then, constructively: what you did not understand; where clarification would help; the research design worksheet questions that do not yet have clear answers (unit? DV? IV? mechanism? variation? alternatives?); suggestions for the survey, data, cases or analysis; a different way of framing the big picture; and something you liked.
Be specific and be kind. “The dependent variable seems to include the independent variable — is regime approval part of how you measure legitimacy?” is a good comment. “It’s interesting” is not.

title: Presenting your work, and being a discussant
text:
In every workshop
Come with reactions. Ask questions of everyone, not just the person you are discussing. Participation is assessed on substance.

title: The short submissions
text:
Four short pieces of writing in Michaelmas Term, worth 15% between them, each one feeding the next. Word limits carry a 10% tolerance either way; outside that range costs up to 5 marks. Within a piece, split the words however is useful — if one idea deserves 250 and another 80, fine.
Each one is submitted to Turnitin in our Blackboard theme area by Tuesday 5pm before the workshop, with the School Assignment Submission Form as the first page, and presented briefly in the workshop from a few slides uploaded to the group OneDrive folder by 8:40 that morning.

title: The short submissions
text:
1. Three potential research questions
2.5% · 400–500 words total · due Tuesday 6 October, 5pm · presented in workshop 2 (8 Oct)
Three brief outlines of questions that could each become your project. For each:

The outcome of interest — your dependent variable, in one plain sentence. What varies, across what units?
A possible explanation — the independent variable you suspect matters.
Why it matters — socially and/or to scholars. Who cares, and why should they?
What it builds on — ideally a paper or two you know of that asked something close, and how yours would extend, test differently or add a nuance.

Indicate an order of preference. It is fine to develop one idea more and sketch the others.
Presentation: one slide per question, five minutes total, twelve minutes with feedback. Say the thoughts out loud — do not paste in your document.
What a good one looks like. Each question has a comparison built in (“does X make Y more likely, across…” rather than “how did Y happen in country Z”), names the units you would compare, and is narrow enough that you can imagine the data or cases in your hands. What a weak one looks like. A topic rather than a question (“censorship in China”), a historical narrative, or a question so big it is a PhD.

title: The short submissions
The short submissions
text:
3. Annotated bibliography
5% · 500 words · due Tuesday 3 November, 5pm · used in workshop 4 (5 Nov)
The key academic research on your question and on your dependent variable. For each item (four to six is plenty in 500 words): what it asks, its main explanation, its method, how it relates to your project, and the strength or limitation you will build on. The important question is whether and how your explanation extends or amends theirs.
Two suggestions:

Search on X and Y separately. What do scholars think causes your Y? What effects does your X have elsewhere? Your combination is new; your X and your Y separately almost certainly are not. Someone has done something similar in another region, or thirty years ago, or with television instead of TikTok — find them and use them as a blueprint.
Read smart and read up. You need not read every word of everything, but you must get the contours. Be guided by prominent work in well-known outlets; if your main source is in an obscure journal you have never heard of, you are probably missing better work. Google Scholar, the Annual Review of Political Science, Oxford encyclopedias, and the literature reviews inside good articles are your friends.

You should be reading far more broadly than what fits in 500 words.
In workshop 4 we do something different: I send each of you a classmate’s final research question; you fill in the research design worksheet about their project and explain it back to them and the group. Bring your own list of open questions too.

title: The short submissions
text:
4. Three potential methodologies
5% · 500 words · due Tuesday 17 November, 5pm · presented in workshop 5 (19 Nov)
Three ways you could answer your question. For each: the method itself; why it suits this question; feasibility, including data sources and whether they exist and are accessible; and how you would implement it. Argue for a preference if you have one.
Some of what I will ask: What is your unit of observation? How is the outcome measured — and does it vary? Is the independent variable measured before the outcome changes? What else could explain the pattern, and what will you do about it? Do you have enough cases (or a large enough N)? If the plan is quantitative: what is the simplest model that answers the question? (Usually a regression. You do not need anything fancier.) If qualitative: what is the comparison, and what would you expect to see if you were wrong?
Presentation: a slide per approach. Data sources with names, not “I will find data”.

title: The short submissions
text:
Then: the research proposal
Compulsory but ungraded · 1,500 words · due Friday 11 December, 5pm
Introduction (topic, social and scholarly significance) · literature review · the variation to be explained · the main posited explanation(s) · the methodological strategy, with data. You get detailed written feedback, and it is the document you work from over the break. Start data collection before Christmas if you possibly can.
